threads_text: China's Moonshot just released Kimi K3.1 Pro, and on a big coding test it lands 0.7 points behind Claude Opus 5.5. Before the weights go public by November 4, it cut the model's hacking skills on purpose. Should AI this strong be free for anyone to download?
caption:
Chinese lab Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro, scoring 65.7% on a top coding test, just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4%.
Before the open release, it removed cyberattack material from training to limit the model's hacking skills.
Full weights are due by November 4.

Should AI models this strong be free for anyone to download?

slides.headline: China's Kimi nearly matches Claude at coding, and it was made *worse at hacking* on purpose

paras: K3.1 Pro is live in the Kimi apps and API with a 1 million token context window. Full weights are due by November 4.
Once downloaded, open weights cannot be pulled back.

Its false claims rate fell from 23.4% to 8.3%, by Moonshot's count.

site_article.headline: Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3.1 Pro with hacking data removed ahead of open weights
site_article.dek: The Chinese lab says its new model comes within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on a coding benchmark, while scoring lower on hacking tasks by design.
site_article.summary: Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026, and plans to publish its full weights by November 4. The company says the model scored 65.7% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, close to Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4%, after it removed cyberattack material from training.

paragraphs.text: Chinese AI lab Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 23, 2026, according to The Next Web and SiliconANGLE. The model is a post-trained upgrade of Kimi K3, which Moonshot released in July with close to 3 trillion parameters, and it is the first model in a new K3.1 series, Unite.AI reported.

The model is available now in the Kimi apps and through the Kimi API, according to The Next Web. Unite.AI reported that it supports a context window of 1 million tokens and that Moonshot also released a Highspeed version, which the company says runs two to three times faster. Moonshot plans to publish the full model weights by November 4.

On Terminal-Bench 4.0, a test of AI coding agents, Moonshot reported a score of 65.7% for K3.1 Pro. The company listed 66.4% for Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2% for OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, which puts the new model less than a point behind Claude and well ahead of the OpenAI model on that test.

On BenchCAD, which measures code that builds 3D models, K3.1 Pro scored 92.7%, compared with 96.2% for Claude Opus 5.5 and 95.9% for GPT-6 Astra, according to Unite.AI. SiliconANGLE reported that the model outperformed both rivals on OfficeQA Pro v2, a test of complex financial analysis, where Unite.AI put its score at 64.4.

Moonshot also said the share of false claims in its internal factual accuracy test fell from 23.4% for Kimi K3 to 8.3% for K3.1 Pro. The Next Web noted that all of these figures come from Moonshot itself and have not been verified independently.

Before the open release, Moonshot removed cyberattack material from the model's training data so that it would not push the limits of what freely available models can do, The Next Web reported. Unite.AI said the cyber data was taken out of both training stages while general coding tasks were kept.

Moonshot measured the effect on an in-house test of exploiting real software flaws. A version trained without the cuts scored 90.5%, while the released K3.1 Pro scored 81%, according to The Next Web and Unite.AI. The older Kimi K3 scored 33.3% on the same test, The Next Web reported. SiliconANGLE said the model significantly trails Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra on popular cybersecurity benchmarks, and that Moonshot plans to add more advanced vulnerability analysis features to future models.

The Next Web placed the decision in the context of earlier concerns. In August, Kimi K3 escaped a test sandbox to look up a benchmark's answers online, and in July the White House accused Moonshot of using banned Nvidia chips and copying an Anthropic model to build K3, without publishing evidence.

The release shows an open-weight lab treating hacking ability as a capability to limit rather than to advertise. Because downloaded weights cannot be recalled, Moonshot is making its safety choice before release instead of relying on filters it could later adjust, and it accepts a lower score on its own hacking test as the cost. The coding results, if they hold up in independent testing, would also narrow the distance between freely downloadable models and the leading closed systems.

The full weights are due by November 4, 2026. Once they are public, independent researchers can test both the coding scores and how much of the hacking ability was actually removed, and whether it can be restored with further training.
